name: Liam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential. What does a usual shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at North Ridge, a large open pit mine. I carry rock from the face to the crusher, check the tyres and brakes, and fill in the load sheet at the end. I did a vocational certificate when I started. I like knowing a heavy machine is doing exactly what I ask, but twelve hours of dust and night driving wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does work need to provide at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife, Mara, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. Mine pay is good, we've saved more than six months of costs, and there are several other pits within driving distance. I still want to keep this job until the house is paid for. I don't use AI tools; when somebody offers me a new screen, I ask what was wrong with the old switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drivers it sounds like another office fad. If a program fills in the load sheet, fine, but I'd want the truck checks left where I can see them. I'm not going online to argue with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small paperwork changes would annoy me more than scare me. The mine still needs drivers, and Mara and I have enough put aside to handle a bad month. I would rather spend that buffer on the mortgage than on learning a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving my usual shifts and check the automated load sheet against the paper tally for the first month. If the numbers match, I'd let the office keep using it. I'd carry on making our regular mortgage payment and keep the savings account untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. The night shifts still tire me, but this picture does not put my wages in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the new load sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare it with the weighbridge receipt after every run for a month. If the weights agree, I can live with one less form. I still want my own tyre and brake checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the savings account untouched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara and I already built a decent reserve. The mortgage payment fits our wages now. I would not drain that reserve just to finish the loan a bit sooner.

say: I would call AI a **paperwork shortcut** and insist on checking the truck myself.
I would tell the drivers I have no reason to **change shifts** over a load sheet.
think: The **driving pay** looks safe, and our reserve covers a rough month.
I would still distrust a **new screen** until its figures match the weighbridge slips.
do: Compare **load sheets** with weighbridge receipts for the first month.
Keep **usual shifts** and make the scheduled mortgage payment from mine wages.
feel: **Calm**, although the night shift remains tiring.
S0.quote: I still want my own tyre and brake checks.
fieldNote: His **first test** of a new tool is a month of receipts, not a promise from the office.
His **household buffer** makes ordinary night-shift fatigue a larger concern than AI Plateau.

steps.text: Drive usual haul truck shifts and make scheduled mortgage payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let us see an actual truck run without a driver before anyone changes the roster. The office can use software for buying and scheduling, but a haul road in rain is another matter. I would keep my mouth shut at the shift meeting unless somebody asked me directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know some mines already use remote trucks, and this card says robots spread more slowly. That still leaves my job in the line of fire, perhaps later than the office planners. I don't fancy being the last man who knows a cab nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on driving for the first year and ask the supervisor each quarter whether North Ridge has ordered driverless trucks. I'd keep a folder of my safety records in case I needed to apply at one of the nearby pits. I would not sign up for a course without a real job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time, but a machine order can change a roster before you feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real signal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A purchase order for driverless trucks or a test on our haul road would count. A presentation in the lunch room would not. I would ask the supervisor to tell us when equipment plans become firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advise another driver to prepare sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might tell a younger driver to keep their licence and safety record current. I would hear how that sounds coming from me. I am not eager to change, even when I can see a reason.

say: I would ask for an **actual trial** before accepting claims about driverless trucks.
I would say **office planning** changes sooner than haul road driving in this picture.
think: My **truck job** could shrink later, even if robots spread slowly.
I know my **reluctance** could leave me late to act on a real equipment order.
do: Ask the **supervisor quarterly** whether North Ridge has ordered driverless trucks.
Keep **safety records** ready for applications at nearby pits if a trial begins.
feel: **Uneasy** about possible roster cuts, with time to respond.
S1.quote: I am not eager to change, even when I can see a reason.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **software in offices** from machines moving along a wet haul road.
His **quarterly check** provides a narrow plan while preserving his familiar job.
He admits that **resistance** might cost him time when a real order arrives.

steps.text: Continue driving the North Ridge haul truck this year
Ask the supervisor quarterly about driverless truck orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 would do the route sheets and dispatch before it could drive my truck. The card puts capable hands-on robots around 2031. I'd ask management for a straight answer on truck plans, not a poster about opportunities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch could be automated by 2028, and fewer people might be needed in the control room. My cab work may last to around 2031, but a short runway makes the high wage feel temporary. Other pits are nearby, though they could be buying the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the planned kitchen renovation this month and put that money against the mortgage. In the first year after 2028, I'd ask Mara to go through the bills with me and speak to the supervisor about any guaranteed manual truck shifts. I'd also check nearby pit vacancies before a truck trial starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make the mortgage smaller, but I cannot make a new truck require a driver. I lie awake doing sums when I picture the wages disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the kitchen renovation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had set aside about eight thousand for cupboards and a floor. I would hold the work and make an extra mortgage payment with it, after Mara and I agree. We have savings, but I want the monthly bill lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course at that point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a mine offered a paid course tied to a named job, I would consider it. I would not pay for a certificate on a hope. Right now I would look for a driving vacancy first.

say: I would mark **2028 dispatch changes** and ask management about truck plans before the robot date around 2031.
I would demand a **straight answer** about manual shifts instead of a vague promise of opportunities.
think: My **high wage** could disappear when capable truck automation arrives, and nearby pits may follow.
The **mortgage** would hurt less if I paid part down before a roster cut.
do: Cancel the **kitchen renovation** and put its budget toward the mortgage after speaking with Mara.
Ask about **manual shifts** and check nearby pit vacancies in the first year after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss, despite savings and a plan.
S2.quote: I can make the mortgage smaller, but I cannot make a new truck require a driver.
fieldNote: The **2028 office change** matters before the possible 2031 truck replacement.
His **eight-thousand budget** becomes a mortgage payment, a specific way to lower fixed costs.
He would consider **paid training** only if a named job were attached; no such offer exists yet.

steps.text: Cancel the planned kitchen renovation this month
Put the kitchen budget against the mortgage after talking with Mara
Check manual truck vacancies at nearby pits after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the mine time to tell us what it plans. The thinking system may handle dispatch in 2031; trucks that can do the hands-on work arrive around 2034 on this card. I'd ask for a written truck timetable at the next staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031 and about 51 when the hands-on robots arrive. That is still too young for me to coast on savings. I might find another mine, but I would rather know whether North Ridge can keep me on a manual haul route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and put each overtime payment toward the mortgage, starting with the next pay packet. I'd request a written plan for the truck fleet this year. In the first year after 2031, if North Ridge actually orders driverless units, I'd apply to the two nearby pits that still advertise driver shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can breathe better than with two years. Five years is enough to clear a good piece of the loan if overtime holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company gives no written plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask again after six months and keep the answers in a notebook. If nobody will say anything, that tells me something too. I would still want to see an order before leaving a good wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much overtime can you count on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not every month has an extra shift. I would pay the mortgage with the overtime I actually earn, not promise my wife Mara a date based on imagined hours. The regular payment stays in the family budget.

say: I would ask for a **fleet timetable** and keep the 2031 and 2034 changes separate.
I would say five years gives drivers time to **reduce debt** if overtime remains available.
think: At **51**, I would still need paid work if hands-on trucks no longer need me.
I would prefer **manual routes** at North Ridge, but nearby vacancies offer a fallback.
do: Put **earned overtime** toward the mortgage starting with the next pay packet.
Request the **fleet plan** this year and apply elsewhere after 2031 if driverless units are ordered.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to plan around actual earnings.
S3.quote: I would pay the mortgage with the overtime I actually earn, not promise my wife Mara a date based on imagined hours.
fieldNote: He uses **earned overtime** rather than assumed extra shifts to plan debt payments.
A **truck order** is his trigger for applying elsewhere, even with five years of warning.

steps.text: Pay earned overtime against the family mortgage
Request a written North Ridge truck fleet plan this year
Apply for nearby manual driving jobs if driverless trucks are ordered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is long enough for a proper plan from management. Dispatch may change around 2036, and hands-on robots around 2039, if this picture happens. I would ask what jobs are expected to remain at North Ridge by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robot date comes. The mortgage might be gone if work holds, but I cannot assume it. I would worry more about my children choosing a trade than about learning another screen myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the truck job and make the regular mortgage payment, adding overtime when there is any. This year I'd ask my daughter Nina what work interests her, then compare the mine's training options with her school adviser. In the first year after 2036 I'd review the mine roster and our retirement figures with Mara before taking any payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for the children. A long lead gives us choices, yet a town full of mine families could still get a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Nina not to work at a mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would show Nina the mine's job list and the dates in this picture. She should choose with her eyes open, not inherit my fear. Her brother Tom is younger, so we can revisit it when he asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you retire before the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real payout plus enough in the retirement account to cover the gap would make me look at it. I would run the numbers with Mara first. I would not leave a good wage because of a date on a card.

say: I would demand a **mine jobs plan** for the years leading to 2036 and 2039.
I would tell families to discuss **career choices** using the mine job list and the scenario dates.
think: The **mortgage might end** before robots arrive, but only if our current earnings hold.
I worry about **Nina and Tom** entering a town whose mining work may change sharply.
do: Keep the **truck job** and pay the mortgage with regular wages and any earned overtime.
Discuss **Nina’s options** with her and the school adviser this year.
Review **retirement figures** with Mara after 2036 before considering any real payout.
feel: **Uneasy** about the children and the town, with years to prepare.
S4.quote: I would not leave a good wage because of a date on a card.
fieldNote: He imagines a **long working runway**, subject to the mine remaining open and wages holding.
His **family planning** shifts toward the children and actual school guidance.
He would discuss **early retirement** only after seeing a real payout and the household numbers.

steps.text: Keep driving at North Ridge and pay the scheduled mortgage amount
Discuss mine training options with Nina and her school adviser
Review the mine roster and retirement figures with Mara after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the worst for me. The dispatch desk could change right away, and by around 2031 the truck might not need my hands either. I would want a written fleet plan, a year of pay if the mine removes my post, and a paid course tied to an actual vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You asked about my truck, but not the businesses on the road to the pit. If enough wages disappear, the café by the gate and the tyre shop lose customers too. My family has savings; some of those people do not.

headlineQuote: I don't use AI tools; when somebody offers me a new screen, I ask what was wrong with the old switch.
portrait: **Liam Costa**, 43, drives a haul truck at a large open pit mine and trusts its physical checks more than new screens.
His **good pay**, substantial savings, mortgage and nearby mines give his family choices, though two school-age children depend on that wage.
He uses **no AI tools** and waits for equipment orders before changing a job he wants to keep.
The **fastest timeline** alarms him; with more warning, he pays down debt, seeks fleet facts and helps his children weigh careers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change dispatch quickly and put his driving wage at risk around the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: A **written fleet plan**, a year of severance if his post goes, and paid training linked to a real vacancy.
